scores.evidence: opener names the winner but the second paragraph buries the verdict in narrative setup rather than sharpest evaluative claim
'He recovered the positions, made the tyres work and, when the race finally brought Russell within reach, completed the pass' — textbook restatement summary
'That left him 12th for the restart and gave Mercedes an opportunity' — bridging sentence doing transitional work a heading should handle
13.7 seconds, 13 seconds, 31 seconds, 0.85s/lap, 0.264s, 0.871s — numbers cluster repeatedly rather than deploying singly
'His late-race pace suggests he would still have caught Russell rapidly' — 'suggests' is correct but the surrounding conditional analysis lacks ownership markers like 'I think' or 'probably'
Russell is consistently the primary benchmark throughout — 'compared with Russell's track position,' teammate delta tracked lap by lap
No quotes, radio messages or official communications appear anywhere in the piece
'He passed his teammate with three laps remaining... The final move settled the race; the circumstances... had been taking shape since lap three' — positional recap posing as interpretation
'Leclerc's early retirement was followed by sixth place for Lewis Hamilton' is flat recounting; no dry irony or juxtaposition deployed for comic/critical effect
No first-person appears at all; no flagged judgment calls or surprise; personality entirely absent
VSC, track limits, green-flag stop used without gloss; Gasly's Alpine pole unremarkable; reader assumed informed
'That does not make the result inevitable in either direction. Traffic, tyre wear...' — this paragraph makes two distinct points and runs slightly long
'A lap later, he was through' is the one punchy sentence; most paragraphs run uniform mid-length without visible variation
VSC mechanism gets room but the Gasly collapse — arguably as significant — gets one throwaway sentence; length doesn't fully track significance

top_fixes: Kill the final paragraph entirely — it restates the argument in three neat clauses, which is the machine's most reliable tell; the piece should end when Antonelli crosses the line or when the Gasly/Ferrari observations close

Insert at least one radio message or team communication as evidentiary punctuation — the VSC call and Antonelli's pit-entry are obvious moments where team audio would complicate or confirm the strategic reading

Break the number-clustering habit: the sequence '13.7 seconds behind... around 13 seconds... roughly 31 seconds' in adjacent paragraphs reads like a data dump; deploy one figure per claim and let the others go
